This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.

This book is for English-speaking learners preparing for ordinary Swedish category B driving. It connects rules with decisions you can explain and practise. It does not grant permission to drive, replace mandatory training or supervised practice, reproduce official examination questions, or guarantee a test result.

Begin with modules 1–3. They establish personal readiness, vehicle preparation and road interpretation. Use modules 4–7 to apply that foundation in traffic and changing conditions. Modules 8–9 develop responsibility for the vehicle, its load and the journey's impact. Module 10 brings the learning together.

Each lesson contains a goal, an explanation, an original worked situation, a knowledge check with its answer, and a short reminder. After each module, write a reflection and use it to plan your next study or supervised practice session. Explain the answer before reading it; then change one condition in the example and consider whether your decision would change.
KörkortGo · How to use this book

Requirements describe applicable duties or conditions, with official references. Official recommendations/advice describe the named authority's guidance. Learning approaches, worked decisions and review guides are original teaching material. They help you apply the principles; they are not additional laws. English explanations are written for learning and do not replace the Swedish legal wording.

References appear beside factual material. Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen provide the main guidance. Official legislation and other public authorities supply details missing from the main agency guidance. Selected manufacturer handbooks supply missing technical cautions and are listed separately. The lessons identify source limits and distinguish recommendations, research and teaching inferences from legal duties. Use the handbook for the actual vehicle; a generic example is not its operating procedure.

Original licensing, examination and vehicle checks are dated 1 October 2026; added passages have their own checks on 12–13 October. Check current official information before using a time-sensitive rule. Hypothetical numbers in examples are identified as such and are not measurements of your vehicle or personal performance.

Driving begins with a choice: whether this person, this vehicle and this journey are ready to go together. Sweden’s Vision Zero (Nollvisionen) aims for no one to be killed or seriously injured in traffic. The choices taught here contribute to that aim. Trafikverket: Vision Zero Learning rules matters, but so does recognising when a different plan is safer. This module helps you build both habits.

This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Your goal: Build a personal preparation checklist covering entitlement, permits, supervised practice, risk training and examinations.

Requirements. For an ordinary new category B licence, you need a valid learner permit, permanent residence in Sweden or at least six months of study here, the minimum age of 18, valid car risk training, and successful theory and practical tests. Holding another EEA licence affects the application route. Category B normally covers a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a registered maximum weight of no more than 3,500 kg; trailers are explained in module 8. Check any conditions on your entitlement, including an automatic-transmission restriction. Transportstyrelsen: category B

Private practice requires an approved supervisor for the particular learner. The learner normally needs a group 1 permit. Practice in a passenger car can begin at 16; the minimum is 17 years and 6 months for practice with a light goods vehicle or a light trailer. The supervisor is legally treated as the driver, must carry proof of approval, and the practice sign must be clearly visible from behind. Exceptions concerning an existing entitlement must be checked against your own circumstances. Transportstyrelsen: category B

Current changes, checked 1 October 2026. The introductory-course requirement for private practice ended on 1 August 2026. Supervisor approval still applies. This change does not remove mandatory risk training. A theory test passed on or after 19 August 2026 is valid for one year. Tests passed before that date retain the earlier rules; Trafikverket describes the ordinary earlier validity as four months. Check your own result and any approved extension rather than adding a year yourself. Supervisor requirements · Risk training · Test validity amendment · Trafikverket: B tests

Risk training has two parts: the first covers alcohol, drugs, fatigue and other risky behaviour; the second covers speed, safety and differing road/weather conditions, including slippery-road training. It must be completed before the tests and remains valid until the licence is obtained or for at most five years. Car and motorcycle risk training are not interchangeable. Transportstyrelsen: risk training

Build your checklist. Record your permit, supervisor approval if practising privately, entitlement conditions, risk-training status, test preparation and any support application. Use actual expiry dates from your records. Schedule practice around skills you need to improve, not only around an available test slot.

Worked decision. Noor plans to practise privately in September 2026. Her relative says no approvals are needed because a course was abolished. Noor checks the current supervisor page and waits for supervisor approval. The removed course and the retained approval are different requirements.
Knowledge check. Does a theory pass from July 2026 automatically become valid for a year?
Remember: Plan the administrative route and the learning route together.
Your goal: Decide whether to drive when tiredness, illness, medication, alcohol or drugs may affect you, and explain a safer alternative.

Requirement. You must not drive when illness, exhaustion, alcohol, other substances or another condition prevents safe control. A legal alcohol threshold is not a guarantee that you are capable of driving safely. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §1

Trafikverket states that the blood-alcohol limit for drink-driving is 0.2 per mille. For an aggravated offence, factors include at least 1.0 per mille, substantial impairment, or driving that creates a clear traffic danger. Non-prescribed narcotics are subject to a zero-tolerance rule. Properly prescribed medication does not make impaired driving acceptable. Trafikverket: drink-driving law · Alcohol, drugs and medication

Alcohol can affect judgement, attention, vision, reactions and coordination. Feeling normal does not measure those effects. Performance can remain impaired the next day. Do not use a fixed number of hours, a shower, coffee or a calculation as a personal clearance to drive. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about medicines and driving; do not change a prescribed treatment simply to make a journey. Trafikverket: effects of alcohol and medicines

Learning approach. Before taking the keys, ask: Can I stay alert? Can I see and move well enough? Has anything changed since I last drove? Can I concentrate on several developing situations? If the answers are uncertain, make a different travel plan and resolve the uncertainty first. Medical eligibility and day-to-day readiness are related but different: having a licence does not mean you are fit for every journey. Medical requirements
KörkortGo · M01-L02 · Sleep and safe judgement

Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness. Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps

Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep. Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. NHTSA: drowsy driving

Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement · NHTSA: stimulant effects

Practice example. Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains unresolved, and a stronger feeling of alertness cannot certify safe judgement. She postpones the drive or arranges an alert driver, and makes time for adequate sleep before driving again.
A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench.
A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench.

Worked decision. A driver has taken a new medicine and feels unusually drowsy. A passenger offers to keep talking to help them stay awake. The safer choice is to arrange another driver or transport and ask for medication advice. Conversation does not resolve the impairment.

Knowledge check. (1) Is driving automatically acceptable if a medicine was prescribed correctly? (2) How does microsleep differ from choosing to close your eyes? (3) A sleep-deprived driver feels energetic and unusually confident after taking a stimulant. Has the missing sleep been remedied, and does that feeling establish safe judgement?
Remember: Decide fitness before deciding convenience.
Your goal: Identify how peers, impulses, confidence and personal circumstances can change a decision, and rehearse a refusal or alternative.

The official education syllabus asks learners to reflect on social influence, impulsive decisions, personal motives and their own limitations. These are skills to practise, not labels to attach to an age group or personality. Category B syllabus, chapter 5

Learning approach. Separate the journey's purpose from the feeling of the moment. “Get everyone home” is a purpose. “Show that I can handle this bend quickly” is a different motive. When a passenger's request changes your speed, following distance or willingness to overtake, name the change before acting on it.

A useful personal boundary is a sentence you can use without debate: “I will stop somewhere safe before changing the route”; “I am not passing here”; or “We need another way home.” These are original rehearsal tools, not official scripts. Practise them before a difficult situation, and agree that passengers will help with navigation only when asked.

Requirement. You still owe care to other road users and must adapt speed to conditions. Cooperation does not authorise ignoring a traffic rule because another person is impatient. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §14

Official policy aim · Vision Zero. Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay. Trafikverket: Vision Zero
A passenger talks to the driver. In the road view, the car remains behind a van near a crest. Illustration, not a scale diagram of following distance.
A passenger talks to the driver. In the road view, the car remains behind a van near a crest. Illustration, not a scale diagram of following distance.

Worked decision. Friends laugh when Amir stays behind a slow vehicle on a road with a hidden crest. He recognises the urge to prove himself, maintains space and waits for a genuinely suitable opportunity. His decision protects the purpose of the trip: arriving safely. There is no need to “win” the interaction.

Knowledge check. (1) Which is better evidence of readiness: feeling confident, or repeatedly identifying hazards and responding safely during supervised practice? (2) Does Vision Zero aim only to reduce minor collisions, or to prevent deaths and serious injuries?
Remember: A decision can be socially uncomfortable and still be the correct driving decision.
Plan the journey before the ignition
Your goal: Compare route, departure time, travel mode and passenger choices for safety, accessibility and environmental impact.

Trafikverket recommends checking forecasts and traffic conditions, allowing time, taking breaks on longer trips and preparing supplies appropriate to the season. The education syllabus also asks you to consider whether a car is the right means of transport and how passengers or timing affect a journey. Journey advice · Syllabus, chapters 4–5

Learning approach. Plan a usable journey rather than an ideal arrival time. Check where you can rest, refuel or charge as appropriate to the vehicle, and stop legally at the destination. Arrange restraints and space for passengers before departure. If the route has unfamiliar junctions or restrictions, identify them while parked.

Compare realistic alternatives. Walking, cycling or public transport may suit some journeys; a car may be necessary for others. Consider access needs, luggage, the return trip and the conditions at the time you will actually travel. A plan that depends on rushing after a late appointment is already fragile.
Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance.
Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance.

Worked decision. A learner and supervisor can practise on a familiar route in daylight or travel through an unfamiliar town during a forecast snow shower. They choose daylight practice today and plan a later lesson for more demanding conditions with suitable preparation. This is staged learning, not an assumption that difficult conditions can always be avoided.
Knowledge check. You are delayed before leaving. What should change first: the arrival expectation or the safety margin?
Remember: Keep a fallback plan that does not depend on taking extra risk.
Three conditions to consider: tiredness, an appointment and worsening weather. No choice is shown.
Three conditions to consider: tiredness, an appointment and worsening weather. No choice is shown.
Scenario: You intend to practise after a long workday, collect a friend and reach an appointment on time. Your supervisor is approved, but the road forecast has worsened.
Explain what you would check before leaving, which circumstances could make you cancel, and how you would respond if your friend urged you to hurry.

Write one decision you are uncertain about, its possible consequences, and the official reference or supervised practice activity that would help. Keep the entry and revisit it after your next practice session. Syllabus self-assessment, chapters 4–5 §3
Answer: No. The amendment has transitional rules for tests taken before 19 August. Confirm the applicable expiry in the official result information.

Answer: (1) No. The driver must still be capable of driving safely. The prescription exception to the narcotics rule does not excuse unsafe impairment. (2) Microsleep is a brief unintended sleep episode, not a deliberate action. (3) No. Adequate sleep addresses sleep deprivation; stimulation can mask fatigue and produce overconfidence without safe judgement.

Answer: (1) Observed performance. Confidence is useful only when it agrees with what you can actually do. (2) Its central aim is that no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. Safer driver choices contribute to that aim.
Answer: The arrival expectation. Inform the people waiting, choose a different mode or postpone if necessary. A late start does not change the rules or stopping space needed.
Review guide: Include legal permission, actual fitness, vehicle/passenger readiness, conditions and a workable alternative. Permission to practise is only one part of the decision.

Prepare a car that is ready
A vehicle check connects what you notice with what you do next. Finding a defect is useful only if you recognise its significance, avoid an unsafe journey and obtain the right help.
M02-L01 · Know what the controls tell you

This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Know what the controls tell you
Your goal: Explain the purpose of core controls, warning indicators, braking and steering systems, and identify when further instructions are needed.

The practical test can include checking steering, brakes, tyres, lighting, fluids and warning systems. You should be able to explain why you check them and propose action if you find a problem. Before moving, adjust the seat, head restraint, steering wheel, mirrors and belt. Trafikverket: safety check

Learning approach. While parked, locate the service brake, parking brake, transmission controls, indicators, lighting controls, wipers, washers, demisting and hazard lights. Explain what each control is for, then demonstrate it with your supervisor. “I can find it” and “I can use it without losing attention” are different learning stages.

The service brake is used to reduce speed and stop; the parking brake helps secure a stationary vehicle. Steering changes the vehicle's direction, but the tyres and road must provide the forces needed to follow that direction. Braking and steering share the available friction: turning the wheel is not proof that the car can follow the intended path. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14 and 50 · VTI friction report, section 4.3

Vehicle-specific boundary. Control layouts, warning meanings and system checks differ. Use the instructions for the actual vehicle before trying an unfamiliar function. This material does not prescribe a universal brake-servo test, fluid-opening procedure or response to every dashboard symbol. An unexplained warning is a reason to establish what is wrong before treating the car as ready.

Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection. Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits

ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer

Recognise a symptom, then act. The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change. Transportstyrelsen: brake inspection · Northern Ireland government: vehicle faults
Pulsating pedal during an emergency ABS stop
Keep firm continuous pressure; steer as needed.
Pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure
Hydraulic leakage or another brake fault
Do not start an unsafe journey; obtain professional help.
Hydraulic pedal feels unusually springy or spongy
Have it checked before moving; do not rely on normal braking.
Wheel imbalance; other faults are possible
Have tyres, wheels and steering assessed; see M02-L02.

What a fuse does. A fuse protects an electrical circuit by interrupting excessive current during an overload or short circuit. Investigate faults under the actual vehicle's instructions. Transportstyrelsen: fuse protection principle
A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown.
A learner consults the vehicle handbook beside a parked car. Establish the actual controls before driving; no universal dashboard layout is shown.

Worked decision. Leila starts a borrowed car and sees a warning she cannot identify. Instead of driving to see whether it disappears, she stays parked, consults the vehicle instructions and seeks help. The lesson is to resolve uncertainty, not to guess from a warning's colour alone.

Knowledge check. (1) Does a familiar selector guarantee familiar operation? (2) Why separate brake circuits? (3) What should you do when the pedal pulsates during emergency ABS braking? (4) What might a sinking or unusually spongy pedal suggest? (5) What does a fuse protect against?
Remember: Learn a function, its limitations and the appropriate response—not only its button.
Your goal: Organise a safety check of tyres, lights, visibility and vehicle condition, and distinguish a defect from a reason to seek help.

Learning approach. Work around the car, then through the driving position. Look for damaged tyres, an unusual stance, leaks or obstructions; confirm that windows and mirrors permit a useful view. Check required lights and indicators, and ask for help where a second person is useful. Check washers and wipers before you need them in poor weather. Use the actual vehicle's instructions for fluid levels and service checks. These groups reflect the official practical-test safety check; they are not a guarantee that a quick walkaround detects every defect. Trafikverket: safety check

Requirements. Tyres must be suitable for the vehicle, including load capacity and applicable speed capability. The registration information and approved vehicle requirements matter when changing tyre sizes. Do not assume any wheel that physically fits is suitable. Transportstyrelsen: tyre requirements

Required lighting must work and be used appropriately. Some cars can run daytime lights without rear lights; the driver must ensure suitable front, rear and side lighting is on in darkness, twilight or poor weather. A trailer's lighting must be on during travel. Automatic settings may need manual intervention. Transportstyrelsen: vehicle lighting

Technical explanation · Steering vibration. Uneven mass distribution around a rotating wheel and tyre can cause steering vibration, sometimes most noticeable at particular speeds. Wheel imbalance is one possible cause, not a diagnosis: tyre damage and other wheel or steering defects may also be involved. Arrange assessment rather than testing the symptom by driving faster. Northern Ireland government: wheel balance and vehicle faults

Vehicle instructions · A temporary spare. Before using a temporary spare, read the actual car and spare-wheel instructions for maximum speed, distance or use restrictions, and required tyre pressure. Follow those limits and replace it with the normal wheel as instructed. Its pressure can differ from the road tyres. Volvo's 2019 V60 Twin Engine handbook gives one model's temporary-use, speed and pressure requirements; these cannot be assumed for every car. Volvo: temporary spare, 2019 V60 Twin Engine
A companion checks the rear of a stationary car and trailer. Check the trailer lights directly before moving.
A companion checks the rear of a stationary car and trailer. Check the trailer lights directly before moving.

Worked decision. A passenger notices that the trailer's rear lights are dark although the car's daytime lights are on. The driver checks the setting and connection before moving. “The dashboard looks normal” is not a check of the trailer lamps.

Practice example. Omar notices vibration on a journey and proposes fitting an unfamiliar temporary spare. He first obtains help to assess the symptom, then checks whether the spare is suitable and reads its limits. Changing a wheel does not establish the original cause. Handling and grip are developed in M07-L02. For hot-coolant precautions during other vehicle checks, see M10-L01.

Knowledge check. (1) Is deep tread enough if a tyre has a defect? (2) What is one possible cause of steering vibration at certain speeds? (3) Which instructions must you check before using a temporary spare?
Remember: Use a repeatable order, then take a specific action for each concern. Detailed winter requirements are in M07-L02.
Your goal: Select suitable restraints for passengers and explain how belts, headrests and airbags work together.

Requirements. In an ordinary car journey, occupants must use an available belt-equipped place and wear the belt. Children under 135 cm normally need an appropriate child restraint. The driver must take appropriate measures to ensure passengers under 15 use the required protection. Limited exceptions exist, including specified short occasional journeys, and should not become a routine travel plan. Seat-belt rules · Traffic Regulation, chapter 4 §§10–10d

For a child aged three or more but shorter than 135 cm, an occasional short transport without an available child restraint is an exception only under the stated conditions: use the belt where possible and not the front seat of a passenger car or light goods vehicle. For a child under three, the exception is an occasional short taxi trip, also excluding the front seat. Plan with the correct restraint instead. Transportstyrelsen: child rules

Official recommendations. Trafikverket recommends rear-facing travel until at least four to five years, preferably longer. Transportstyrelsen's advice says as long as possible, normally around four. These are recommendations, not a single legal birthday on which to turn the seat. Choose equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits. Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit. Trafikverket: children in cars · Transportstyrelsen: child protection

Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person occupying the seat. Children in cars · Airbags · Seats and head restraints

Technical explanation · Head restraints. In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. Trafikverket: seats and head restraints

Why children face backwards. A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. Trafikverket: child head and neck protection · Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection

Controlled deformation. Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones

Practice example. A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle structure have different roles that work together.

An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions.

An adult and child stand beside an open rear door. The empty booster and rear bench face forwards. This scene does not demonstrate installation or belt fit; follow the child-restraint and vehicle instructions.

Worked decision. A child reaches the legal height threshold, but the belt still lies badly. The adult checks an appropriate approved booster rather than treating the threshold as an instruction to discard it.

Knowledge check. (1) Is a rear-facing seat safe in front of an active airbag for a short trip? (2) What does a head restraint do? (3) Why does rear-facing travel protect a small child? (4) Why are crumple zones designed to deform?
Remember: Legal minimums, official recommendations and equipment compatibility answer different questions.
Your goal: Plan observation and control for starting, stopping, reversing, hill starts and turning, and explain why supervised practice is needed.

Requirements. Before moving away from the edge, changing position or lane, you must ensure the movement can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. Turning around and reversing must be possible without danger or obstruction to other road users. Signal your intention where required, but a signal does not give you priority. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43, 46 and 65–66

Learning approach. Break a manoeuvre into preparation, observation, controlled movement and reassessment. Choose a place with enough room; check around the vehicle and along the intended path; move only while the space remains safe. Stop and reassess when the view changes. Looking once before starting is not continuous observation.

A hill start is a control task: prevent unintended movement while coordinating the actual vehicle's transmission, brakes and accelerator. Do not copy pedal sequences between cars without instruction. Reversing, parking and turning also need practical feedback about vehicle dimensions and the path followed by its corners. The official practical test may examine these skills, including effective braking. Practise braking exercises only in suitable, supervised conditions—not as an experiment in ordinary traffic. Trafikverket: manoeuvring and braking
The driver is in the left-hand seat and looks around before moving. Controls are illustrative; learn the actual vehicle.
The driver is in the left-hand seat and looks around before moving. Controls are illustrative; learn the actual vehicle.
A car and van occupy adjacent bays. A pedestrian is on the footway between the bays and the access lane. Consider what the driver may lose sight of. Diagram not to scale.
A car and van occupy adjacent bays. A pedestrian is on the footway between the bays and the access lane. Consider what the driver may lose sight of. Diagram not to scale.

Worked decision. While reversing into a space, a driver loses sight of a person who was beside the car. The driver stops. The empty camera image is not enough to resolve where the person went; direct observation and an adequate overall view are still needed.
Knowledge check. If you have signalled and started moving, must another road user always make room?
Remember: Slow control gives you opportunities to observe and stop; it does not remove the need to look.

Scenario: You will drive an unfamiliar car with a child passenger, then reverse out of a confined space.
Describe your preparation and the point at which you would stop and seek help.
Record one control or check you can explain but cannot yet perform reliably. Arrange supervised practice and review the result. Syllabus self-assessment, chapter 2 §3

Answer: (1) No; establish operation while stationary. (2) A remaining circuit can retain some braking after one fails, with reduced capability. (3) Keep firm continuous pressure and steer as needed; normal ABS pulsation is not a reason to pump. (4) Sinking can suggest a hydraulic leak or fault; sponginess can suggest air. Obtain professional assessment before an unsafe journey. (5) Excessive current; the fuse interrupts the circuit.

Answer: (1) No; condition and suitability also matter. Have the defect assessed. (2) Wheel imbalance is one possibility; assessment is needed because other faults can cause vibration. (3) The actual vehicle/spare maximum speed, distance or use restrictions, and required pressure; no universal limit can be assumed.

Answer: (1) No. Trip length does not make it safe. (2) It helps limit damaging head movement and reduce neck-injury risk, particularly in rear impacts. (3) The seat supports the relatively heavy head and body together and takes collision forces, protecting the vulnerable neck. (4) Controlled deformation absorbs energy and slows the compartment more gradually, reducing occupant forces.
Answer: No. Your obligation to check safety remains throughout the manoeuvre.

Review guide: Establish control operation, vehicle condition, restraint and airbag compatibility, visibility and a safe manoeuvre plan. Do not improvise a technical check or reverse into an uncertain space.

This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Your goal: Classify the main sign families and describe the decision each one prompts.

Start with purpose, then read the specific symbol and any supplementary panel. The official catalogue groups signs by function. Do not rely on colour alone: similar shapes can communicate different duties, and some important signs have distinctive shapes. Transportstyrelsen: sign catalogue

Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h.

These are learning questions, not substitutes for the individual sign descriptions. A warning of children, for example, does not assign a new numerical speed by itself; your speed must still allow safe control and a response to foreseeable hazards. A posted maximum speed is a ceiling, not a demand to maintain that speed. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 2 · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15

Requirements. B1 means yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. Make that intention clear early and proceed only without danger or obstruction. B2 requires a stop before entering the crossing road or track area. Stop at the stop line; without one, stop immediately before the signal or before entering the crossing road or track area, as applicable. A rolling pause does not meet a stop duty. Your goal: Interpret signs, panels, markings and signals together, including authorised directions.

Requirements. Follow the traffic instructions that apply to you. Where an instruction differs from a general traffic rule, the instruction governs. A steady traffic-light indication takes precedence over a yield or stop sign; a police officer's direction takes precedence over the rules and ordinary traffic instructions. This is not a rule that a green signal cancels every other restriction. Authorised guards also give traffic directions that must be followed. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §§2–4
Separate examples. A static picture does not show the complete movement; read the description and the official instruction.

P1 · Police stop instruction — front and rear

Traffic approaching the officer from the front or rear must stop; traffic approaching from the sides may proceed. The officer's continuing orientation matters even after the arm movement. Officer faces the viewer with one arm extended sideways.
Police stop instruction — palm facing you. Officer raises a palm towards approaching traffic.
P2 · Police stop instruction — palm facing you

The guard identifier must be worn on the front and back. It identifies the role rather than giving a separate movement instruction. Garment identification panel bearing VAKT.

For ordinary vehicle signals: red means stop; red and amber together still mean stop, with green approaching. Green permits movement, subject to other duties and space ahead. Amber means stop unless, when green changes to amber, you are already so close that stopping would be dangerous. Flashing amber requires particular caution; read the signs and applicable rules. Arrow signals apply to the direction indicated. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 3 §§3–6
Red, red/amber, green and amber appear in that order. Flashing amber is a separate condition, not the next stage of the normal cycle. Arrow indications apply to the direction shown.

Proceed with particular caution and apply the other instructions and traffic rules. Flashing is not demonstrated by the still image. Amber flashing lamp represented by a still drawing.

A red lane-control cross closes the lane; a green downward arrow allows its use; a diagonal amber arrow tells you to move in the indicated direction. Make any lane change safely. Signals for pedestrians or public transport are not automatically instructions for your car. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 3 §§7–15

Markings. A broken centre or lane line identifies a boundary; it does not promise that overtaking is safe. A warning line indicates that crossing is unsuitable because of conditions and may precede a continuous line. Continuous lines and hatched areas have crossing restrictions, with specified exceptions such as a necessary passage around an obstruction under particular caution. A painted line is not an invitation to improvise an exception. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 4, M1/M3/M8/M9 · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§9–11
Read the marking on your side
For paired lines, identify the line immediately beside your side of the road. The line on the far side does not grant you permission to cross.
Centre or lane line. Two examples of a broken white line on a dark road background.

A broken line separates opposing directions or adjacent lanes, depending on its position. It does not guarantee that crossing or overtaking is safe. Two examples of a broken white line on a dark road background.

Crossing this line is unsuitable because of the traffic conditions. It may also warn of a continuous line ahead. Long white strokes with short gaps.

Your goal: Explain how observation, speed, reaction, braking, grip and following space affect your options.

Requirements. Choose a speed that preserves control and lets you stop within the road you can see and before a foreseeable obstruction. Your distance from the vehicle ahead must allow for it slowing or stopping. Weather, visibility, road condition, vehicle condition and loading all matter. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14–16

For an ordinary car, the general speed limits are 50 km/h within a built-up area and 70 km/h outside it, unless another applicable limit has been prescribed. The motorway default is 110 km/h; 120 km/h can be prescribed. Local and road-specific limits often differ, and a lower vehicle-combination limit still applies. Read the current signs and conditions rather than selecting a speed from the road’s appearance. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §17, chapter 4 §20 and chapter 9 §1

Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. Trafikverket: speed and impact · VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3

Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.

Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition.

Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method

Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye.
KörkortGo · M03-L04 · Time and braking distance

Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response

Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop.

Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation

Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car.

Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value.

Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time.

Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model.

Rough total: S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard.

Source and assumption limits. Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions.
Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts. Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input.
Example A · 40 km/h and 0.5 seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 4. Reaction R = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6 m. Braking B = 4² × 0.4 = 6.4 m. Total S = 6 + 6.4 = 12.4 m. The half-second input affects reaction, not braking.

Example B · 70 km/h and one second. First v ÷ 10 = 7. Reaction R = 7 × 1 × 3 = 21 m. Braking B = 7² × 0.4 = 19.6 m. Total S = 21 + 19.6 = 40.6 m. Squaring seven gives 49; do not multiply speed itself by 0.4.

Example C · 50 km/h and two seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 5. Reaction R = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m. Braking B = 5² × 0.4 = 10 m. Total S = 30 + 10 = 40 m. Doubling reaction time doubles this model's reaction estimate, leaving braking unchanged.

Compare separately with exact conversion. At 50 km/h and two seconds, exact constant-speed reaction distance is (50 ÷ 3.6) × 2 = about 27.8 m, compared with the shortcut's 30 m. Dividing the shortcut factor 0.3 by the exact conversion factor 1 ÷ 3.6 gives 1.08: an 8% overestimate for reaction distance. Mixing 27.8 m with rough braking of 10 m gives about 37.8 m, not the exercise model's 40 m. Keep exact conversion separate from the rough-model answer.

Try the approximate process. Calculate reaction, braking and total for (A) 30 km/h and 0.5 seconds, (B) 80 km/h and one second, and (C) 100 km/h and two seconds. Give each part in metres, check the square, then add. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section.

KörkortGo · M04-L02 · Waiting to turn left

Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight. When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. New York DMV: waiting to turn left

Waiting is different from turning. Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving.

Practice example. Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. On rural roads, use M06-L01 to assess bends, crests and other risks before choosing a turning opportunity.

This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
See the person behind the movement
Your goal: Anticipate the needs of different road users without assuming that everyone sees, hears or moves as you do.

Requirements. Show particular consideration for children, older people, school patrols and people whose disability or illness is apparent and affects their use of traffic. Reduce speed appropriately near children, stopped passenger transport and other situations with foreseeable risks. Give pedestrians sufficient room and time when meeting or passing them. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §1 and chapter 3 §§15 and 58

Learning approach. Look for the space a person needs, not only the space they occupy now. A child may be hidden by a parked car. A cyclist may need to move out from an obstruction. A wheelchair user may need a usable kerb transition. You cannot reliably infer someone's hearing, vision or intentions from a quick glance. Allow time and observe their movement rather than demanding a response through the horn.
Children, cyclists and riders have different needs. Sensory-impairment panels are separate examples; absence of a sign does not prove absence of risk.

Horses and riders also belong in your traffic assessment. Vehicle rules apply to riding and leading horses in relevant respects; they are not simply pedestrians because they travel slowly. Give them an unhurried, spacious interaction, and avoid unnecessary noise. This is a cautious application of the general duty of care, not a fixed passing-distance rule. Transportstyrelsen: horses in traffic
This warning supports early observation. It does not specify a fixed passing distance.
Horse riders ahead. Horse and rider inside a warning triangle.

Bus rule. Where the maximum permitted speed is 50 km/h or lower, a driver approaching a bus whose driver signals to leave a bus stop must slow and give it the opportunity to leave, stopping if needed. The bus driver must also take particular care. If passing on the right of a bus or tram stopped at a stop without a refuge, stop to allow boarding or alighting passengers free passage. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§45 and 58
Recognise a bus stop and speed limit
The bus-stop marker and the 40 km/h speed sign are independent examples. The bus marker itself does not set the speed limit.
Bus stop. White bus on a blue rectangular sign.

Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 40: maximum 40 km/h.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 40: maximum 40 km/h.

Bus comparison · Check the road limit. The threshold concerns the maximum permitted speed on the road, not how fast you happen to be travelling. At a 70 km/h limit, the special bus-stop departure rule above does not apply. The bus must wait for an entry that can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. You still have a duty to adapt speed to facilitate an observed entry into your lane. A bus indicator does not create unconditional priority, and the higher road limit does not excuse deliberately blocking it. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–45
Duties when the bus signals to leave its stop
Slow and let the bus leave; stop if needed. The bus driver must take particular care.
70 km/h, ordinary entry into your lane
The special bus-exit duty does not apply. The bus waits for a safe entry; you adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry.

Safety advice · Let a guide dog work. Do not pet, call to or talk to a working guide dog to attract its attention. Distraction can endanger the person it is helping. Allow the pair room and time; if you need to communicate, address the handler rather than trying to direct the dog. The handler chooses the route and remains in control. For example, a passenger beside your parked car wants to greet a guide dog at a crossing. Ask them to leave it working and keep the path clear. MFD: meeting a working guide dog

Traffic terminology · A bicycle is a vehicle. A person riding an ordinary pedal bicycle is operating a vehicle, even without an engine. “Vehicle” does not mean only “motor vehicle”. Apply the relevant cyclist duties and protections; crossing distinctions remain in M04-L03. Transportstyrelsen: bicycle definition
Leave room for the bus and people

The bus signals to leave its stop. The full-width middle lane remains separate from the opposing lane. In the worked decision the road limit is 40 km/h; available road width does not remove the bus duty.

The bus signals to leave its stop. The full-width middle lane remains separate from the opposing lane. In the worked decision the road limit is 40 km/h; available road width does not remove the bus duty.

Worked decision. On a 40 km/h street, a bus signals out. You ease speed early and leave room rather than trying to squeeze past. You also watch for people near the stop; making space for the bus is not your only task. Compare an otherwise ordinary 70 km/h road: the bus waits for a safe entry, while you still adapt speed to help an observed entry into your lane. Travelling at 40 on that 70 road does not activate the special bus rule.

Knowledge check. (1) Does a narrow visible gap beside a cyclist prove passing is safe? (2) A bus signals from its stop on a 70 km/h road while you drive at 40. Does the special bus rule apply, and what must both drivers do? (3) Should you greet a working guide dog? (4) Is a person riding a pedal bicycle operating a vehicle?

Your goal: Distinguish ordinary streets from pedestrian streets, walking-speed areas and cycle streets.

Requirements. On a pedestrian street (gågata) and in a walking-speed area (gångfartsområde), drive no faster than walking pace and yield to pedestrians. The general rule prohibits parking; a specifically signed lawful parking arrangement must be assessed on its own terms. Walking pace is a condition to match, not a universal speedometer number. Special streets · Traffic Regulation, chapter 8 §1 and chapter 10 §1

Motor vehicles may use a pedestrian street only to cross it, apart from the specified necessary journeys: goods to or from shops or equivalent premises; goods or residents to or from addresses there; guests to or from hotels or equivalent premises; and sick people or people with mobility impairments to or from an address. A convenient shortcut does not qualify. Check additional signs and local restrictions. Traffic Regulation, chapter 8 §1

On a cycle street (cykelgata), the maximum is 30 km/h, and motor vehicles must adapt speed to bicycle traffic. Vehicles entering from another road yield to vehicles already on it. Parking is restricted to specially provided places. When leaving a cycle street for another road, the exit yielding rule applies. Special streets · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §21 and chapter 8 §1a

Choose a lawful place to stop
Your goal: Distinguish stopping from parking and interpret the rules, signs and time panels for a proposed place.

Parking is leaving a vehicle stationary for a reason other than traffic conditions, avoiding danger, boarding or alighting, or loading or unloading goods. Remaining behind the wheel does not automatically make waiting “stopping.” Nor does switching on hazard lights create permission. Transportstyrelsen: stopping and parking
Compare no parking with no stopping and parking. An extent marking needs its actual accompanying restriction; it does not create permission.

Core requirements. Do not stop or park where you create danger, unnecessarily obstruct traffic or hide a sign or signal. Normally use the right side in your direction of travel; one-way roads and specified rail-track situations have exceptions. Secure the vehicle against rolling and prevent unauthorised use. Open doors only without danger or unnecessary inconvenience. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§47, 50 and 52

Learning approach. Select a place that offers both a safe entry and a safe departure. Check the full route of the vehicle: front corners can move sideways while you watch behind. Stop when information is lost. If you need to inspect the area, first secure the vehicle and choose a safe way to do so. Your goal: Identify risks from bends, crests, narrow roads, animals and slow vehicles and justify speed and position changes.

Requirements. Keep right when meeting another vehicle and leave a safe lateral gap. If an obstruction on your side prevents a safe meeting, stop if necessary to let the approaching vehicle pass. Your speed must suit the visible road and foreseeable hazards, with particular care at bends, crests and narrow meetings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15 and 30

Learning approach. Read the road in sections: the visible straight, the entry to a bend, the portion hidden behind a crest and the next place someone might join. Never extend the clear section in your imagination. A vehicle emerging from a field or a cyclist beyond a bend changes what seemed to be an empty road.

A wildlife fence can be interrupted by access points and does not remove the need to observe. Trafikverket: wildlife

Turn planning · Choose a safer approach. On an ordinary two-way rural road, heavy traffic may make a direct left turn unsafe. Continue to a suitable, permitted place or route where you can change direction safely, then return to approach the destination with a right turn if that movement is allowed and safe. This can avoid hazardous waiting and crossing the opposing stream at the original entrance. It is a planning alternative, not permission to turn around immediately on the carriageway. If no safe legal return route exists, choose another route or postpone. Trafikverket: example of routing to a turning place

Legal boundary. Before turning or leaving the road, protect oncoming traffic and traffic on the road you enter; take particular care of following traffic. A turnaround must cause neither danger nor obstruction. Signs and access restrictions still apply. Never turn around or reverse on a motorway or expressway. If you can wait safely and legally for a left turn, remember the advice in M04-L02 to keep the front wheels straight; that advice does not make an unsafe turn suitable. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§24, 26, 29 and 46; chapter 9 §§1–2

Worked rural alternative. A farm entrance is on your left and busy traffic leaves no safe opportunity. You continue to an accessible junction route that legally and safely brings you back in the opposite direction. The entrance is then on your right. Check people, traffic and the entrance again before turning; the revised route does not guarantee a safe final movement.

Wildlife observation · Time and terrain. Give extra attention at dawn and dusk, near animal habitats and where fences end or have openings. Scan woodland edges, bushes and small waterways beside the road: Trafikverket's road-project study describes these as animal routes that can conceal an approach. Its national guidance also describes animal passages through fence openings. These are cues for observation and speed planning, not predictions that animals only cross there. Trafikverket: wildlife and fence passages · Trafikverket: habitat example, page 9

Apply the cues. At dusk, woodland meets a field beside a gap in the fence. Read the edges and opening as possible animal approaches, and choose speed for the view and foreseeable hazard. Keep observing even on fenced stretches. Prevention belongs here; actions after a wildlife collision are in M10-L02.

Narrow bridge: the obstruction is on the teal driver’s right and the van approaches in its own lane. Reduce speed before the narrowing and stop if necessary. The scene does not measure a safe lateral gap.

Narrow bridge: the obstruction is on the teal driver’s right and the van approaches in its own lane. Reduce speed before the narrowing and stop if necessary. The scene does not measure a safe lateral gap.

Worked decision. You approach a narrow bridge with a van coming towards you and an obstruction on your side. You reduce speed before the narrowing and stop if necessary. Do not move into the van's path simply because you reached the obstruction first.

Knowledge check. (1) No vehicle is visible beyond a crest. Is the road proved clear? (2) Heavy traffic makes your rural left turn unsafe. What alternative can you plan? (3) Which time and roadside cues call for extra wildlife attention?
Remember: Let what you can actually see determine the available space.
Your goal: Compare waiting with overtaking using visibility, speed difference, space and a safe completion path.

Requirements. Overtake only without danger and with sufficient clear road. Do not start when a following driver has begun overtaking, or pass on the left when the vehicle ahead signals an intended leftward movement. Leave safe lateral clearance and a safe return opportunity. When being overtaken, do not increase speed or otherwise make the pass harder. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§31–38

The normal passing side is left. Exceptions include a vehicle turning or clearly preparing to turn left, and the specified rules for marked same-direction lanes on roads limited to 70 km/h or less. Passing in queues or destination lanes has separate provisions; it does not remove the need to protect people at crossings. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§7, 31 and 41–42

Restrictions to recognise. Overtaking is generally prohibited immediately before or in a road junction, with specified exceptions for right-side overtaking, police/signal control, or an established yielding/stopping duty on the crossing road. Similar restrictions apply at level crossings, with exceptions for barriers or road-junction-type traffic signals. At an obscured bend or crest, do not use an opposing lane to overtake; the detailed provision contains limited exceptions. Section 39 also contains an exception for passing two-wheeled vehicles without sidecars. That exception does not override the danger prohibition, continuous-line restrictions or the uncontrolled-crossing prohibition. None of these exceptions proves a manoeuvre safe. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §39

Do not overtake immediately before or on an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, uncontrolled cycle passage or cycle crossing. Where parallel-lane passing is legally not classified as overtaking, the special crossing rule still requires a speed allowing an immediate stop for a person on the crossing or passage. Obey signs and continuous-line restrictions as well. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§11, 40–41

Requirements. Motorways are for eligible motor vehicles and combinations designed and permitted to travel at least 40 km/h; class I mopeds are excluded. This is an eligibility condition, not a command to maintain 40 km/h in a queue. Enter and leave through the designated starts, ends and access routes. Do not reverse, turn around, use the central divider or cross-connections, or stop outside designated parking/rest areas except as an unavoidable incident requires. The relevant restrictions also apply to expressways (motortrafikled) and their access routes. Traffic Regulation, chapter 9 §§1–2

In an acceleration lane, adapt speed to the traffic in the lane you intend to join and enter as soon as it can be done without danger or unnecessary obstruction. A safe joining movement is your responsibility; other drivers who notice the intended entry must adapt speed to facilitate it. Entry without an acceleration lane has a yielding rule. For an exit, take the suitable lane in good time and enter the deceleration lane as soon as possible. If you miss the exit, continue to a permitted exit and re-plan; never reverse to recover it. A breakdown is dealt with in M10-L01, not by using the shoulder as a convenient place to check navigation.

After the motorway · Recheck your speed. After a long period at a steady motorway speed, your perception can adapt to that pace. On a slower road, the correct lower speed may feel unusually slow. This effect is often called speed adaptation or velocitation. Check the speedometer regularly to judge actual speed and adjust to the current limit and conditions. The feeling alone is not evidence that the speedometer is faulty. ODOT: speed perception and speedometer checks

Worked transition. After a long motorway trip, you leave onto a road signed 50 km/h. At 50, the car feels as if it is crawling. Confirm the speedometer reading, read the new road and retain a speed suited to its limit, visibility and hazards. Do not accelerate merely to recover the motorway's familiar feeling.

Railway requirements. Approach with particular care and at a speed that allows a stop before the crossing. Do not enter when a train or tram is approaching, a red signal shows, an audible warning sounds, a barrier is lowering, lowered or rising, or you might have to stop on the tracks. Cross without unnecessary delay only when it is permitted and there is room beyond. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §7

Two different emergencies. Trafikverket says that if warnings begin while you are already crossing, continue out. If a functioning vehicle is trapped between the barriers, drive through the barrier to leave the tracks. If the vehicle has broken down on the tracks, evacuate everyone promptly, move well away and call 112. Give the crossing ID from the crossbuck sign if available without returning to danger. Do not stay on the tracks attempting a repair or pushing exercise. Trafikverket: level-crossing safety

Roadworks. Expect changed lanes, reduced speeds, workers and queues. Follow the current signs, signals and authorised guard directions; allow room around work areas and keep distance. A familiar road may now have a different usable path. Temporary guidance deserves attention before you reach the first barrier, not after you have entered the work area.
